[[File:Isotonic regression.svg|thumb|400px|An example of isotonic regression (solid red line) compared to linear regression on the same data, both fit to minimize the [[mean squared error]]. The free-form property of isotonic regression means the line can be steeper where the data are steeper; the isotonicity constraint means the line does not decrease.]]
{{Regression bar}}
In [[statistics]] and [[numerical analysis]], '''isotonic regression''' or '''[[monotonic]] regression''' is the technique of fitting a free-form line to a sequence of observations such that the fitted line is [[non-decreasing function|non-decreasing]] (or non-increasing) everywhere, and lies as close to the observations as possible.

== Applications ==
Isotonic regression has applications in [[statistical inference]]. For example, one might use it to fit an isotonic curve to the means of some set of experimental results when an increase in those means according to some particular ordering is expected. A benefit of isotonic regression is that it is not constrained by any functional form, such as the linearity imposed by [[linear regression]], as long as the function is monotonic increasing.

Another application is nonmetric [[multidimensional scaling]],<ref>{{Cite journal | doi = 10.1007/BF02289694 | author = Kruskal, J. B. | year = 1964 | title = Nonmetric Multidimensional Scaling: A numerical method | journal = Psychometrika | volume = 29 | issue = 2| pages = 115–129 | s2cid = 11709679 | author-link = Joseph Kruskal }}</ref> where a low-dimensional [[embedding]] for data points is sought such that order of distances between points in the embedding matches [[order of dissimilarity]] between points.  Isotonic regression is used iteratively to fit ideal distances to preserve relative dissimilarity order.

Isotonic regression is also used in [[probabilistic classification]] to calibrate the predicted probabilities of [[Supervised learning|supervised machine learning]] models.<ref>{{cite conference
 | last1 = Niculescu-Mizil | first1 = Alexandru
 | last2 = Caruana | first2 = Rich
 | editor1-last = De Raedt | editor1-first = Luc
 | editor2-last = Wrobel | editor2-first = Stefan
 | contribution = Predicting good probabilities with supervised learning
 | doi = 10.1145/1102351.1102430
 | pages = 625–632
 | publisher = Association for Computing Machinery
 | series = ACM International Conference Proceeding Series
 | title = Proceedings of the Twenty-Second International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2005), Bonn, Germany, August 7–11, 2005
 | volume = 119
 | year = 2005}}</ref>

Isotonic regression for the simply ordered case with univariate <math>x, y</math> has been applied to estimating continuous dose-response relationships in fields such as anesthesiology and toxicology. Narrowly speaking, isotonic regression only provides point estimates at observed values of <math>x.</math> Estimation of the complete dose-response curve without any additional assumptions is usually done via linear interpolation between the point estimates.<ref name=StylFlour02>{{cite journal |last=Stylianou|first=MP |author2=Flournoy, N|author2-link=Nancy Flournoy |title=Dose finding using the biased coin up-and-down design and isotonic regression |journal=Biometrics |year=2002 |volume=58 |issue=1 |pages=171–177 |doi=10.1111/j.0006-341x.2002.00171.x|pmid=11890313 |s2cid=8743090 }}</ref>

Software for computing isotone (monotonic) regression has been developed for [[R (programming language)|R]],<ref name=cir>{{cite web |last1=Oron |first1=Assaf |title=Package 'cir' |url=https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/cir/index.html |website=CRAN |publisher=[[R Foundation for Statistical Computing]] |access-date=26 December 2020}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Leeuw|first1=Jan de|last2=Hornik|first2=Kurt|last3=Mair|first3=Patrick|title=Isotone Optimization in R: Pool-Adjacent-Violators Algorithm (PAVA) and Active Set Methods|journal=Journal of Statistical Software|date=2009|volume=32|issue=5|pages=1–24|doi=10.18637/jss.v032.i05|issn=1548-7660|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|last1=Xu |first1=Zhipeng |last2=Sun|first2=Chenkai |last3=Karunakaran |first3=Aman |title=Package UniIsoRegression |url=https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/UniIsoRegression/UniIsoRegression.pdf |website=CRAN |publisher=R Foundation for Statistical Computing |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260110075342/https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/UniIsoRegression/UniIsoRegression.pdf |archive-date=10 Jan 2026| url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name="Turner23"/> [[Stata]], and [[Python (programming language)|Python]].<ref>{{cite journal|first1=Fabian|last1=Pedregosa|display-authors=etal|title=Scikit-learn:Machine learning in Python|journal=Journal of Machine Learning Research|date=2011|volume=12|pages=2825–2830|bibcode=2011JMLR...12.2825P|arxiv=1201.0490}}</ref>

== Problem statement and algorithms ==
Let <math>(x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_n,y_n)</math> be a given set of observations, where the <math>y_i \in \mathbb{R}</math> and the <math>x_i</math> fall in some [[partially ordered set]].  For generality, each observation <math>(x_i,y_i)</math> may be given a weight <math>w_i \ge 0</math>, although commonly <math>w_i=1</math> for all <math>i</math>. 

Isotonic regression in the <math>L_2</math> metric seeks a weighted [[least-squares]] fit <math>\hat{y}_i \approx y_i</math> for all <math>i</math>, subject to the constraint that <math>\hat{y}_i \le \hat{y}_j</math> whenever <math>x_i \le x_j</math>.  This gives the following [[quadratic programming|quadratic program]] (QP) in the variables <math>\hat{y}_1, \ldots, \hat{y}_n</math>:

:<math>\min \sum_{i=1}^n w_i (\hat{y}_i - y_i)^2</math> subject to <math>\hat{y}_i \le \hat{y}_j \text{ for all } (i,j) \in E</math>

where <math>E = \{(i,j): x_i \le x_j\}</math> specifies the partial ordering of the observed inputs <math>x_i</math> (and may be regarded as the set of edges of some [[directed acyclic graph]] (dag) with vertices <math>1,2,\ldots n</math>).  Problems of this form may be solved by generic quadratic programming techniques.

In the usual setting where the <math>x_i</math> values fall in a [[totally ordered set]] such as <math>\mathbb{R}</math>, we may assume [[WLOG]] that the observations have been sorted so that <math>x_1 \le x_2 \le \cdots \le x_n</math>, and take <math>E = \{(i,i+1): 1 \le i < n\}</math>.  In this case, a simple and efficient [[iterative algorithm]] for solving the quadratic program (of a "least squares" optimisation in the <math>L_2</math> metric) is the [[pool adjacent violators algorithm]]. Conversely, Best and Chakravarti<ref name="BestEtAl2019">{{Cite journal|last1=Best|first1=Michael J.|last2=Chakravarti|first2=Nilotpal|date=1990|title=Active set algorithms for isotonic regression; A unifying framework|url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1007/bf01580873|journal=Mathematical Programming|volume=47|issue=1–3|pages=425–439|doi=10.1007/bf01580873|s2cid=31879613 |issn=0025-5610|url-access=subscription}}</ref> studied the problem as an [[Active-set method|active set]] identification problem, and proposed a primal algorithm. These two algorithms can be seen as each other's dual, and both have a [[computational complexity theory|computational complexity]] of <math>O(n)</math> on already sorted data.<ref name="BestEtAl2019" />

To complete the isotonic regression task in the <math>L_2</math> metric, we may then choose any non-decreasing function <math>f(x)</math> such that <math>f(x_i) = \hat{y}_i</math> for all i.  Any such function obviously solves
: <math>\min_f \sum_{i=1}^n w_i (f(x_i) - y_i)^2</math> subject to <math>f</math> being nondecreasing
and can be used to predict the <math>y</math> values for new values of <math>x</math>.  A common choice when <math>x_i \in \mathbb{R}</math> would be to interpolate linearly between the points <math>(x_i,\hat{y}_i)</math>, as illustrated in the figure, yielding a continuous piecewise linear function:
:<math>f(x) = \begin{cases}
                 \hat{y}_1 & \text{if } x \le x_1 \\
                 \hat{y}_i + \frac{x-x_i}{x_{i+1}-x_i}(\hat{y}_{i+1}-\hat{y}_i) & \text{if } x_i \le x \le x_{i+1} \\
                 \hat{y}_n & \text{if } x \ge x_n
              \end{cases}</math>

It is possible -- but more time-consuming -- to compute an isotonic regression in a metric other than <math>L_2</math>.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Stout |first1=Quentin F. |year=2008|title= Unimodal regression via prefix isotonic regression |journal=Computational Statistics & Data Analysis |volume=53 |issue=2 |publisher=Elsevier |pages=289-297 |doi=10.1016/j.csda.2008.08.005}}</ref>  An <math>L_1</math> fit has a [[least absolute deviation]] and may thus be more robust to large outliers than an <math>L_2</math> fit with its [[least squares]] criterion.

Another generalisation is to [[unimodality |unimodal]] regressions, i.e. to fits with a non-decreasing segment followed by a non-increasing segment (or vice versa).<ref name="Turner23">{{cite web |last1=Turner |first1=Rolf |title=Unimodal isotonic regression, Iso::ufit() |url=https://search.r-project.org/CRAN/refmans/Iso/html/ufit.html |publisher=CRAN |year=2023 |access-date=18 August 2026}}</ref>

== Centered isotonic regression ==

As this article's first figure shows, in the presence of monotonicity violations the resulting interpolated curve will have flat (constant) intervals. In dose-response applications it is usually known that <math>f(x)</math> is not only monotone but also [[Smoothness|smooth]]. The flat intervals are incompatible with <math>f(x)</math>'s assumed shape, and can be shown to be biased. A simple improvement for such applications, named centered isotonic regression (CIR), was developed by Oron and Flournoy and shown to substantially reduce estimation error for both dose-response and dose-finding applications.<ref name=OronFlour17>{{cite journal |last=Oron|first=AP |author2=Flournoy, N |title=Centered Isotonic Regression: Point and Interval Estimation for Dose-Response Studies |journal=Statistics in Biopharmaceutical Research |year=2017 |volume=9 |issue=3 |pages=258–267 |doi=10.1080/19466315.2017.1286256|arxiv=1701.05964 |s2cid=88521189 }}</ref> Both CIR and the standard isotonic regression for the univariate, simply ordered case, are implemented in the R package "cir".<ref name=cir/> This package also provides analytical confidence-interval estimates.
